1658: When you meet an elder, you should wait for them to wai first.
When you meet an elder, you should lower your head a little first.
When you meet an elder, you should greet them by name first.
1659: If a child wais you, you should wai back the same way — that is only polite.
If a child wais you, a smile is enough in return — you needn't say anything.
If a child wais you, you must always wai back — never just nod in reply.
1660: With friends your own age, you just say their nickname — no need for 'khun'.
With friends your own age, a wai is only for saying goodbye — not hello.
With friends your own age, you still wai the first time you meet — never after that.
1661: Before class begins, the students will stand up for the teacher.
Before class begins, the teacher will greet the students first.
Before class begins, the students will recite a short prayer.
1662: Don't call someone older than you by their nickname; use their full name instead.
Don't call someone older than you 'pi' at work; use their job title instead.
Don't call someone older than you by name in public; wait for them to speak first.
1663: When we meet a stranger, we just call them 'khun' until we know them better.
When we meet a stranger, they will usually call us 'pi' or 'nong' first.
When we meet a stranger, we just use their name with 'khun' in front.
1664: Someone of high status, we address as 'khun'.
Someone of high status, we greet with a deep wai.
Someone of high status, we never address by name.
1665: When you start a new job, you should let the senior staff speak first.
When you start a new job, you should learn everyone's nickname first.
When you start a new job, you should wai your manager every morning.
1666: Thai children are taught to wai their teachers every morning.
Thai children are taught to respect their grandparents from a young age.
Thai children are taught to greet their teachers before every lesson.
1667: Let the elders serve themselves first, then take what you want.
Let the elders sit down first, then bring the food to the table.
Let the elders take the best pieces, then help yourself.
1668: When you have to walk in front of an elder, you should ask to pass first.
When you have to walk in front of an elder, you should pass on their left side.
When you have to walk in front of an elder, you should slow down a little.
1669: When I meet your parents, should I bring them a gift?
When I meet your parents, do they have to wai me first?
When I meet your parents, do I call them 'khun pa'?
1670: You take your shoes off before going into a temple, right?
You take your shoes off before sitting down to eat, right?
You take your shoes off before going into the kitchen, right?
1671: Don't pat a Thai person's head playfully — not even a friend's — because the head is sacred.
Don't pat a Thai person's head in greeting — not even a child's — because it is disrespectful.
Don't pat a Thai person's back to hurry them — not even a child's — because it seems rude.
1672: Don't point your feet at people — and at an elder, even less so.
Don't point your feet at a doorway — and at a Buddha image, even less so.
Don't point your feet at a shrine — and at a monk, even less so.
1673: Don't step over someone who's sitting, or over their bag.
Don't step over someone who's sleeping, or wake them suddenly.
Don't step over someone who's eating, or reach across them.
1674: When entering someone's house, take your shoes off — don't leave them on.
When entering someone's house, greet the eldest first — don't go straight in.
When entering someone's house, stand on the threshold — don't step over it.
1675: When you beckon someone over, wave with your whole hand, not one finger.
When you beckon someone over, raise your hand slowly, not quickly.
When you beckon someone over, use your right hand, not your left.
1676: Don't point your finger at a shrine — it looks disrespectful.
Don't point your finger at people — it draws bad luck.
Don't point your finger at a monk — it looks improper.
1677: Thai banknotes carry the King's image, so don't fold one in half.
Thai banknotes carry the King's image, so don't hand one over with your left hand.
Thai banknotes carry the King's image, so don't write anything on one.
1678: Before the film starts, the cinema plays the royal anthem, and most people stay seated quietly.
Before the film starts, the cinema plays the royal anthem, and everyone removes their hat.
Before the film starts, the cinema shows a short royal film, and most people stand to show respect.
1679: When people go out to eat together, the bill is usually shared equally.
When people go out to eat together, the youngest usually pours the drinks.
When people go out to eat together, the eldest usually orders for everyone.

1659.q: If a child wais us, we do not need to wai back — just a nod to acknowledge is enough.
1659.nat: If a child wais you, you don't have to wai in return — just nodding back is enough.

1660.q: With friends of the same age, you do not need to wai — it's fine; just to greet is enough.
1660.nat: With friends your own age, you don't need to wai — just a greeting is enough.

1661.q: Before entering the study class, the students will wai the teacher first.
1661.nat: Before class begins, the students will wai the teacher first.

1662.q: Don't call someone who has much more age than you by name alone; you should call them 'pi' (older sibling) or 'lung' (uncle) instead.
1662.nat: Don't call someone older than you by name alone; call them 'pi' or 'lung' instead.

1664.q: We call someone of high status 'than' — it's an honorific.
1664.nat: Someone of high status, we address as 'than'.

1668.q: When you have to walk past in front of an elder, you should stoop down a little.
1668.nat: When you have to walk in front of an elder, you should stoop down a little.

1669.q: When I meet your father and mother, do I have to wai them?
1669.nat: When I meet your parents, do I have to wai them?

1670.q: To enter a Thai person's home, you must take your shoes off first, right?
1670.nat: You take your shoes off before going into a Thai home, right?

1671.q: Don't pat a Thai person's head playfully — even a child, you shouldn't — because the head is a sacred thing.
1671.nat: Don't pat a Thai person's head playfully — not even a child's — because the head is sacred.

1672.q: Don't point your feet at people — and at a Buddha image even more so; you really shouldn't.
1672.nat: Don't point your feet at people — and at a Buddha image, even less so.

1673.q: Don't walk over the body of someone who is lying down, or walk over food.
1673.nat: Don't step over someone who's sleeping, or step over food.

1674.q: When entering the house of someone else, you should step over the threshold — don't tread on it.
1674.nat: When entering someone's house, step over the threshold — don't tread on it.

1675.q: When you call someone to come over to you, you should beckon with your hand face down — don't turn your hand up.
1675.nat: When you beckon someone over, wave with your palm down, not palm up.

1676.q: Don't use your index finger at people — it will look impolite.
1676.nat: Don't point your finger at people — it looks impolite.

1677.q: Thai banknotes have the King's image on them, so don't step on a note that fell.
1677.nat: Thai banknotes carry the King's image, so don't step on a dropped note.

1678.q: Before the film shows, in the building they will play the royal anthem, and most people will stand to show respect.
1678.nat: Before the film starts, the cinema plays the royal anthem, and most people stand to show respect.

1679.q: When they go to eat together, the one who is more senior is usually the one who pays.
1679.nat: When people go out to eat together, the more senior one usually pays.
